scenes.animation: Zippy holds up a paragraph about his grandmother that reads only 'She is nice. She is good. She is very nice.' The page yawns, stretches and falls asleep on the desk.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: I described my nani. She is nice, she is good, she is very nice. Why is my page snoring?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Because it tells, but it doesn't show. A descriptive paragraph should let the reader see the person.

scenes.animation: A task card slides in: 'Descriptive Paragraph | 100 to 120 words | a person, event or situation | visual or verbal cue | 5 marks | choose 1 of 2'. Each part lights up in turn.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In your Class 9 paper, you write a descriptive paragraph of 100 to 120 words, based on a picture or a few verbal cues.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It carries five marks, and you choose one out of two questions.

scenes.animation: A portrait of Nani is painted layer by layer: silver hair and round spectacles (appearance), a hand stirring halwa (habits), a group of neighbourhood children around her (qualities), a warm glow in the narrator's heart (impression). Labels pop beside each layer.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Build the person in four layers. First, appearance: my nani has silver hair and round spectacles that slide down her nose.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Second, habits and actions: every Sunday, she stirs a pot of halwa and hums old songs.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Third, qualities, with an example. Fourth, your own feeling about the person.

scenes.animation: A see-saw: on one side 'She is kind' (light, floats up); on the other 'She saves the first roti for the stray dog at our gate' (heavy, sinks down). Label: 'Show, don't just tell'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So instead of she is kind, I say she saves the first roti for the stray dog at our gate?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exactly. One real detail is worth three adjectives.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Use vivid words, and keep one tense, usually the present for a person you know well.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Describe a person who has inspired you, using the cues: appearance, nature, what you learnt.' A three-part plan appears: 'Opening line | Body: cues in order | Closing impression'. A sticker: 'EXAM TIP: use every cue'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A common question: describe a person who inspires you, with cues given.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: an opening line that introduces the person, then cover each cue in order, then a closing line about their effect on you.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: examiners check that every cue is used. A missing cue means missing content marks, so tick them off as you write.

scenes.animation: Recap board with Nani's portrait, now wide awake and smiling. Points appear: '1. 100 to 120 words, from visual or verbal cues', '2. Appearance, habits, qualities, impression', '3. Show with details; cover every cue'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: a descriptive paragraph is 100 to 120 words, based on cues.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: build appearance, habits, qualities and your impression.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: show with real details, and cover every cue.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My nani's halwa deserves at least 120 words.

name: Descriptive Paragraph: Describing an Event or Situation

scenes.animation: A school sports day. Zippy's report floats above: 'Sports day happened. It was fun. Then it ended.' A disappointed trophy slumps on the podium.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Sports day happened, it was fun, then it ended. That covers everything, right?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That covers nothing. When you describe an event, the reader should feel they were standing in the crowd.

scenes.animation: Five senses icons orbit the stadium: an eye (colourful flags), an ear (whistles and cheering), a nose (the smell of wet grass), a tongue (cold lemonade), a hand (a sweaty baton). Each icon drops a phrase onto the page.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Use the senses. What did you see, hear and smell? Colourful flags fluttered, whistles shrieked, and the smell of wet grass filled the air.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Sense details turn a list of facts into a scene.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: So I should mention the cold lemonade after my race?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes, if it helps the reader taste the moment with you.

scenes.animation: A timeline arrow builds across the page: 'Setting (when, where)' -> 'Main moments in order' -> 'Your feeling at the end'. Small icons appear: a calendar, a relay race, a smiling face.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Organise it in order. Start with the setting: when and where it happened.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then describe the main moments in sequence, and end with how you felt or what it meant.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Beginning, middle, feeling. Like a mini movie.

scenes.animation: A monsoon street scene flickers in as a second example: 'a situation'. Rain floods a road; children float paper boats; a scooter splashes through. Past-tense verbs light up: 'poured', 'floated', 'splashed'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A situation works the same way. For a flooded street after heavy rain, describe the scene, the people's reactions, and the mood.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: For a past event, stay in the past tense from start to finish. Switching tenses is a common error.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Describe the Annual Day celebration of your school in 100 to 120 words.' A plan builds: 'Date and venue | Chief guest, performances | Best moment | Your feeling'. A 'EXAM TIP' sticker: 'Title + word limit'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A likely question: describe your school's Annual Day.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: date and venue, the main performances, one special moment in detail, and your feeling at the end.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: stay close to 120 words. Going far beyond the limit wastes time and adds errors.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the trophy standing proud again. Points appear: '1. Use the five senses', '2. Setting, moments in order, feeling', '3. Keep one tense; respect the word limit'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: use sense details to bring the scene alive.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: move from setting to main moments to your feeling.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: keep one tense and stay within the word limit.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The whistle shrieked, the crowd roared, and Zippy won the sack race. Allegedly.

scenes.animation: A campfire at night. Zippy tells a story: 'Once upon a time there was a boy. Then he found a box. The end.' The campfire sputters out in boredom.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Once there was a boy, he found a box, the end. Why did the fire go out?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Your story has no problem, no suspense and no ending worth waiting for. Let's rebuild it.

scenes.animation: A task card: 'Story Writing | 100 to 120 words | on a given cue or title | 5 marks | choose 1 of 2 (story or diary entry)'. Then a story mountain rises: 'Beginning -> Problem -> Climax -> Resolution'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: In your paper, you write a story of 100 to 120 words from a given opening line or title. It is five marks, with a choice between a story and a diary entry.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Every good story climbs a mountain: a beginning, a problem, a climax, and a resolution.

scenes.animation: The cue appears: 'Rohan opened the old tin box and gasped.' The mountain fills in: a dusty attic (beginning), a faded map and a note (problem), a race to the old banyan tree (climax), grandfather's childhood letters found (resolution).

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Suppose the cue is: Rohan opened the old tin box and gasped. Start from exactly that line.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Build a problem: inside is a faded map pointing to the old banyan tree. Climax: he digs there as it begins to rain.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Resolution: he finds his grandfather's childhood letters, a treasure of a different kind.

scenes.animation: Tool badges clip onto the story: 'Title', 'Past tense', 'One line of dialogue', 'Clear ending'. A short speech bubble from Rohan appears: 'Dadaji, these are yours!'

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Can I add dialogue?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Yes, one or two short lines make a story lively. But keep the story in the past tense, and give it a title.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: With only 120 words, use one main event and just two or three characters.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Complete the story: "It was the day of the final match, and our best player was missing..."' A checklist ticks: 'Use the cue as given', 'Title', 'Conflict and ending', 'Word limit'. Sticker: 'EXAM TIP'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: complete a story from a cue about a missing player on match day.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: continue from the cue, raise the tension, and solve the problem clearly by the end.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: do not change the given cue or its characters. Examiners check that your story grows out of it.

scenes.animation: Recap board by the relit campfire. Points appear: '1. 100 to 120 words from a cue or title', '2. Beginning, problem, climax, resolution', '3. Title, past tense, short dialogue'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: write 100 to 120 words, starting from the given cue or title.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: climb the mountain: beginning, problem, climax and resolution.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: add a title, keep the past tense, and use a little dialogue.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: And the fire is back. That's how you know it's a good story.

scenes.animation: Zippy's diary lies open with a padlock. Inside, it reads like a timetable: '7 am: woke. 8 am: school. 2 pm: lunch.' The diary's lock pops open and the diary sighs 'Tell me how you FELT!'

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My diary is complaining. I wrote down everything I did today!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A diary is not a timetable. It is a private talk with yourself about what happened and how you felt.

scenes.animation: A diary page builds its format piece by piece: 'Day and date' top left, 'Time' (optional) beside it, 'Dear Diary' salutation, body paragraphs, and a signature at the end. Each piece clicks into place.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Format first. Write the day and date at the top. Many students also add the time.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then Dear Diary, if you like, the body, and your name or initial at the end.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The word limit is 100 to 120 words, and it shares its choice with story writing.

scenes.animation: A three-step staircase: 'What happened' (a result card in hand), 'How I felt' (a heart swinging from nervous to proud), 'What I learnt or will do next' (a lightbulb). Zippy hops up each step.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Organise the body in three steps. What happened. How you felt about it. What you learnt, or what you will do next.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Like: today I got my maths result, I was nervous, then thrilled, and now I will practise geometry more.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Perfect shape.

scenes.animation: Language tags flutter around the diary: 'First person: I, me, my', 'Informal but correct', 'Past tense for events; present for feelings now'. A red cross appears over slang like 'lol' and 'gr8'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Write in the first person. The tone is personal and informal, but the grammar must still be correct.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Events of the day go in the past tense; feelings you have now can be in the present. And no text-message slang.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'You helped an injured stray puppy on your way home. Write a diary entry about the experience.' A plan appears: 'Date | the incident | your feelings | reflection on kindness'. Sticker: 'EXAM TIP: feelings carry marks'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Likely question: write a diary entry about helping an injured stray puppy.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: the date, the incident briefly, your feelings in detail, and a reflection on kindness.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: many students only narrate the event. Feelings and reflection are what make it a diary entry.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the diary, now happily locked again. Points appear: '1. Day, date, Dear Diary, signature', '2. What happened, how I felt, what I learnt', '3. First person, informal, correct'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: format with the day and date, Dear Diary and your name.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: write what happened, how you felt, and what you learnt.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: use the first person, an informal tone, and correct grammar.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Dear Diary, today I learnt how to write to you. You're welcome.

scenes.animation: An exam paper with a long passage stretches like a scroll down to the floor. Zippy starts reading word by word, and cobwebs slowly grow on him while the clock spins fast.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: This passage is so long, I grew cobwebs just reading it!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: That's the discursive passage. It is 400 to 450 words, but a smart plan makes it quick.

scenes.animation: A label pops up: 'Discursive passage = the writer discusses an issue or gives an opinion'. Example title: 'Should mobile phones be allowed in schools?' Arrows mark 'for' and 'against' points in the text.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A discursive passage discusses an issue, gives opinions and argues. For example, whether mobile phones should be allowed in school.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The questions test comprehension, interpretation, inference, evaluation and vocabulary. It carries ten marks.

scenes.animation: A three-step strategy slides in as footprints: 'Step 1: read the questions first', 'Step 2: skim the passage for the main idea', 'Step 3: scan back for each answer'. A highlighter marks key lines.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Step one: read the questions first, so you know what to look for.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Step two: skim the passage quickly to get the main idea and the writer's view.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Step three: go back and scan the exact lines for each answer.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Underline the topic sentence of each paragraph. It tells you where each idea lives.

scenes.animation: Two question types split: 'Inference: why does the writer say...?' (a detective magnifying glass), 'Vocabulary: find a word that means...' (a dictionary). A small hint card: 'Answer from the passage, not your opinion'.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: What if the answer is not written anywhere?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Then it is an inference question. Use clues in the passage to work out what the writer means, but never add your own opinion.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: For vocabulary, look near the paragraph number given, and match the part of speech.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. Which word in paragraph 2 means "harmful"?' Zippy picks a verb; it bounces off. Neo taps the adjective 'detrimental' and it glows. Sticker: 'EXAM TIP: match the part of speech'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Try: which word in paragraph two means harmful?

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Harmful is an adjective, so the answer must be an adjective too. Detrimental!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: in short answers, write complete, precise sentences and don't copy long chunks of the passage.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the scroll neatly rolled up. Points appear: '1. Discursive: 400 to 450 words, issue or opinion', '2. Questions first, skim, then scan', '3. Infer from clues; match part of speech'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the discursive passage is 400 to 450 words about an issue or opinion.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: read the questions first, skim for the main idea, then scan for answers.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: infer from clues, and match the part of speech in vocabulary questions.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: No more cobwebs. I'm a scanning machine now.

scenes.animation: A passage appears with a bar chart attached showing 'Hours of screen time per day' for different age groups. Zippy stares at the bars and says 'Why is there maths in my English paper?'

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: Bars and percentages in English? Did someone mix up the papers?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: No mix-up. This is the case-based factual passage. It comes with a chart or data, and you read both together.

scenes.animation: A task card: 'Case-based factual passage | 200 to 250 words | visual input: statistical data or chart | 10 marks'. The passage and chart slide side by side, connected by glowing lines.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: It is a factual passage of 200 to 250 words, with a visual input like a table or chart. It carries ten marks.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: The text explains the facts, and the chart shows numbers. Many questions need both.

scenes.animation: A chart-reading drill: the title glows first, then the axis labels, then the legend, then the tallest and shortest bars get star stickers. Label: 'Title, axes, highest, lowest, trend'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Read the chart in order. First its title, then what each axis or column shows, then the units.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Next, spot the highest, the lowest and the overall trend. Is it rising, falling or steady?

scenes.animation: A question card: 'According to the chart, which group spends the most time on screens?' Zippy points to the wrong bar; the bar blinks 'check the label!'. Neo points to the correct bar, and the matching sentence in the passage lights up too.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: The longest bar is the answer. Easy!

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Only if the question asks for the most. Some ask for the least, or the difference between two values. Read the question word carefully.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: And check that the passage and chart agree before you answer.

scenes.animation: An exam card: 'Q. Based on the data, what conclusion can be drawn?' The answer builds: 'Trend + one figure as evidence'. Sticker: 'EXAM TIP: quote the number and its unit'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: A likely question: what conclusion can be drawn from the data?

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Answer approach: state the trend in one sentence, and support it with one figure from the chart.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Exam tip: always write the unit, like percent or hours. A number without its unit can cost you the mark.

scenes.animation: Recap board with the bar chart now wearing a tiny graduation cap. Points appear: '1. 200 to 250 words + chart or data', '2. Title, axes, units, highest, lowest, trend', '3. Answer with evidence and units'.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Recap. One: the case-based passage is 200 to 250 words with a chart or data.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Two: read the title, axes and units, then the highest, lowest and trend.

lines.speaker: NEO
lines.text: Three: support every answer with evidence, and always write the unit.

lines.speaker: ZIPPY
lines.text: My screen time chart? Let's not read that one.
